tip: Shops really did shut at midday: τα μαγαζιά έκλειναν (ta magaziá éklinan = the shops used to close) for the afternoon rest – many small shops still do.
No 'of' after fear verbs – φοβάμαι (fováme) takes the thing directly: φοβόταν τη βροχή (fovótan ti vrochí = was afraid of the rain).
The ongoing past sets the scene, the one-off past interrupts: διάβαζα (diávaza = I was reading) when ήρθε (írthe = came) cuts in.
ξαφνικά (xafniká = suddenly) is a signal word – it flips the sentence to the one-off past: χτύπησε (chtýpise = it knocked), not the ongoing form.
περίμενα μισή ώρα (perímena misí óra) can mean 'I waited' or 'I was waiting' half an hour – the two past forms coincide here, so context decides.
για usually means 'for', but after speech verbs it's 'about': μιλούσαμε για σένα (miloúsame gia séna = we were talking about you).
Background weather takes the ongoing past: έκανε κρύο (ékane krýo = it was cold); the one-off event gets the simple past – βγήκαμε (vgíkame = we went out).
The object pronoun sits inside the future phrase: θα σε πάρω (tha se páro = I'll call you) – σε (se = you) slots between θα (tha) and the verb.
Greek asks for forgiveness rather than 'apologizing': θα της ζητήσω συγγνώμη (tha tis zitíso signómi = I'll ask her for forgiveness).
κλείνω (klíno) literally means 'close' – Greek closes what it books: θα κλείσω τα εισιτήρια (tha klíso ta isitíria = I'll book the tickets). Tables too.
Greek passes time instead of having it: θα περάσουμε τέλεια (tha perásume télia) is literally 'we'll pass perfectly' = we'll have a great time.
After να (na) the negative is μην (min), not δεν (den): για να μην έχει κίνηση (gia na min échi kínisi = so there's no traffic).
θα βαφτίσουμε (tha vaftísume = we'll baptize) announces a big family event – traditionally the godparent, not the parents, picks the baby's name.
μπορεί να (borí na) is a frozen 'might/maybe' – different from personal μπορώ (boró = I can): μπορεί να βρέξει (borí na vréxi = it might rain).
A reservation goes 'in the name', not under it: στο όνομα (sto ónoma = in the name) is the set phrase for giving your booking.
παίρνω (pérno = take) is the ordering verb: τι θα πάρετε; (ti tha párete = what will you take?) is how waiters ask what you'll have.
πάει (pái = it goes) does the pricing work here: πάει με το κιλό (pái me to kiló), literally 'it goes with the kilo' = it's priced by the kilo.
Putting εγώ after the verb adds emphasis: πληρώνω εγώ (pliróno egó = I'm the one paying). Handy, since Greeks genuinely compete for the bill.
χωρίζουμε τον λογαριασμό (chorízume ton logariasmó = shall we split the bill) is understood, but the custom leans to one person treating the whole group.
Bare να (na) + verb gives friendly advice: να πας (na pas = you should go) – no 'should' word needed, the να carries it.
λείπει ένα πιρούνι (lípi éna pirúni = a fork is missing) – λείπει covers absent people too: λείπει ο Νίκος (lípi o Níkos = Nikos is away).
Greek arrives 'with delay': με δύο ώρες καθυστέρηση (me dýo óres kathistérisi = with two hours' delay) is the standard way to say 'two hours late'.
An adjective does the work of a whole English phrase: ήρθα όρθιος (írtha órthios), literally 'I came upright' = I rode standing the whole way.
Duration needs no 'for': κοιμήθηκα όλο το ταξίδι (kimíthika ólo to taxídi = I slept the whole trip) – the time span just follows the verb bare.
Greek marries 'with' someone, not to them: παντρεμένη με έναν γιατρό (pandreméni me énan giatró = married with a doctor).
θυμάμαι (thimáme = I remember) looks passive with its -μαι (-me) ending, but the meaning is plain active – a whole family of Greek verbs works this way.
Greek takes a phone to call someone: πήραμε τηλέφωνο (pírame tiléfono), literally 'we took a phone' = we phoned.
Σκέφτομαι συχνά (skéftome sichná = I often think) – another verb wearing the passive-style -μαι (-me) ending with a fully active meaning, like θυμάμαι (thimáme).
Time-when needs no preposition: το μεσημέρι (to mesiméri = at midday) is just article + noun. Same for το βράδυ (to vrádi = in the evening).
το τραπέζι (to trapézi) is both the table and a dinner party – so στο τραπέζι (sto trapézi) here means coming to the dinner, not the furniture.
χρειάζομαι (chriázome = I need) wears the passive-style -μαι (-me) ending too, and you'll use it daily: χρειάζεται να (chriázete na) = it needs to.
-αίνω (-éno) builds 'get X-er' verbs from adjectives: ακριβός (akrivós = expensive) → ακριβαίνουν (akrivénun = they're getting more expensive).
η σακούλα (sakúla) is the shopping or carrier bag – a handbag is η τσάντα (tsánda), so the two don't swap.
-άς (-ás) turns a place into its person: περίπτερο (períptero = kiosk) → περιπτεράς (peripterás = kiosk owner).
Greek has no infinitive: 'I want to try' becomes θέλω να δοκιμάσω (thélo na dhokimáso), literally 'I want that I try'.
ο χασάπης (hasápis) is what people say for the butcher – κρεοπωλείο (kreopolío) is the formal word on the shop sign.
-πωλείο (-polío) = shop that sells: άνθος (ánthos = flower) → ανθοπωλείο (anthopolío = flower shop). Spot the suffix and shop signs decode themselves.
The -ονται (-onde) ending means 'get X-ed' with no helper verb: κουράζονται (kurázonde = they get tired) – no 'become' or 'get' word needed.
Order έναν διπλό ελληνικό (énan dipló ellinikó = a double Greek coffee) by sweetness: σκέτο (skéto = plain), μέτριο (métrio = medium), γλυκό (glykó = sweet).
το στέκι (stéki) is a friend group's fixed hangout – the café or bar where your παρέα (paréa = group of friends) always ends up.
κλείνω (klíno = close) is the booking verb for appointments too: έκλεισα ραντεβού (éklisa randevú = I booked an appointment).
Body states use -ομαι (-ome) for 'get': ζαλίζομαι (zalízome = I get dizzy), σηκώνομαι (sikónome = I get up) – no 'get' word needed.
Greek has a verb for being late: άργησα (árgisa = I was late) says it alone, and the amount follows bare – άργησα δέκα λεπτά (déka leptá = ten minutes).
μη (mi) + verb makes a prohibition: μη φας (mi fas = don't eat) – no helper verb needed, μη does all the work.
θα περάσει (tha perási = it will pass) means once and done – θα περνάει (tha pernái) would mean it keeps happening. Same verb, two futures.
